design_detail: Systematic review with narrative synthesis (PRISMA-guided; no registered protocol reported; no meta-analysis) of English-language randomized controlled trials of any medication, alone or with psychosocial treatment, for amphetamine or methamphetamine dependence or use disorder, searched to 19 June 2019 in PubMed, EMBASE, CINAHL and Scopus. 43 trials (4065 participants, 23 medications or combinations) are tabulated with dose, duration, population, design and results; risk of bias was judged on listed features rather than with a standard tool.
can_establish: What medications had been tested in randomized trials for amphetamine or methamphetamine dependence up to mid-2019, how those trials were designed (small, outpatient, mostly male, high non-completion, heterogeneous outcomes, sparse harm reporting) and that none produced convincing evidence of efficacy.
cannot_establish: The size of any medication's effect (no pooling and few effect sizes are reported), whether any agent is ineffective (absence of signal in small trials), or the comparative safety of the medications (only 3 of 43 trials reported adverse-event information, by the review's count); its ranking of 'most consistent' signals is a narrative judgment that the tabulated primary outcomes do not support.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable at review level. Included trials were run in outpatient settings (32, 74.4%), inpatient settings (5, 11.6%), both (4) or unreported settings (2); in the USA (23, 53.5%), Iran (7), Australia (4), Malaysia (2), Thailand (2), Finland, Finland and New Zealand, Iceland, Russia and Sweden (1 each); 26 single-site and 16 multi-site (Table 2).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: randomized controlled trials, any age or sex, testing a medication alone or with psychosocial treatment for amphetamine or methamphetamine dependence or use disorder, reporting an outcome on amphetamine or methamphetamine use, associated symptoms (craving, withdrawal) or retention. Excluded: human laboratory studies, studies enrolling primarily people not dependent on amphetamine or methamphetamine, animal and qualitative studies, reviews and secondary analyses; English language only (Methods, 2nd paragraph).
sample.demographics: 2858 of 4065 participants (70.3%) were men; 9 trials enrolled men only. 30 trials enrolled people dependent on methamphetamine only, 4 methamphetamine or amphetamine, 4 amphetamine only, 3 amphetamine-type stimulants with opioids, 2 methamphetamine or cocaine. Trials were published between 1994 and 2019 (the text says 1995; reference 36 is from 1994).
sample.attrition: In the 38 trials reporting completion, 2298 of 3733 randomized participants completed (61.6%), so 38.4% did not; adherence was not reported in 11 trials (25.6%) and ranged from 21% to 100% where reported (Results › Study Selection; Risk of Bias; Outcomes and Measures).
sample.selection_effects: 34 trials (79.1%) excluded people with depression or psychotic disorders or taking antidepressants or antipsychotics, and women were 29.7% of participants, so the evidence describes mostly men without psychiatric comorbidity. Several positive signals come from defined subgroups (men who have sex with men; people using less than daily; Iranian men in residential or inpatient settings).

exposure.measurement: The exposure is each trial's assigned medication; doses and durations as given in Table 4 are study conditions (for example dexamphetamine 60 mg or 110 mg daily, methylphenidate 54 mg daily, naltrexone 50 mg orally, 380 mg by monthly injection or a 1000 mg implant, bupropion 300 mg daily, mirtazapine 30 mg daily, topiramate 200 mg daily, modafinil 200 to 400 mg daily). Treatment periods ranged from 7 days to 24 weeks.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only; see Table 4 of the review. Participants' baseline frequency of use varied across trials, and trials defined 'low use' as 5, 10 or 18 of the past 30 days (Discussion › Limitations).
exposure.polysubstance: Most trials excluded other substance dependence; three enrolled people with combined amphetamine-type stimulant and opioid dependence (results sometimes pooled across drugs), and one enrolled people on methadone. The review identifies exclusion of polydrug use as a limit on generalizability.

comparison.controls: Placebo in 39 trials by the review's count; the remainder used treatment as usual, low-dose active control (imipramine 10 mg) or another active drug. One included trial (buprenorphine versus methadone) had no placebo or untreated control at all.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same populations as the active arms.

outcomes.instruments: As used by the trials: urine drug screens (41 of 51 uses of an abstinence primary outcome, analysed 16 ways, with cut-offs from 78 to 1000 ng/mL), self-report (timeline followback, drug diaries, days of use), hair analysis, craving scales (VAS, Brief Substance Craving Scale, cocaine craving questionnaires), withdrawal scales (AWQ, ACSA, ASSA), dependence scales (ASI, SDS, LDQ), depression, retention and adherence measures (Table 5).
outcomes.validity_norms: The review documents low concordance between self-reported adherence and objective measures (74% by self-report versus 42% by electronic caps in one trial; 74.7% versus 48.5% in another).
outcomes.operationalization: Efficacy was any reported effect on use, associated symptoms or retention; the review does not prioritize primary over secondary or post hoc results when describing 'signals'.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable at review level (no statistical synthesis). The trials used 55 distinct primary outcome measures 93 times and 75 secondary outcome measures 158 times, so many signals come from multiple secondary analyses.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable at review level. Title, abstract and full-text screening by two reviewers independently with a third for disputes; extraction by two reviewers on identical spreadsheets compared for consistency (Methods, 4th paragraph).

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled estimates. The review reports few effect sizes: bupropion, post hoc in people with light baseline use, odds ratio 2.8 for an MA-free week (p < 0.0001; Shoptaw 2008); subgroup odds ratios 1.39 and 1.34 (p <= 0.001) in men with low baseline use and 1.27 (p = 0.02) in non-depressed women with low baseline use (Elkashef 2008). Otherwise results are given as directions of significance. Descriptive aggregates: 61.6% completion; 70.3% men; 3 of 43 trials (7%) reporting adverse-event information; adherence 21% to 100%.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; the paper states it follows PRISMA reporting.
analysis.selective_reporting: Trial-level risk-of-bias judgments, the extended study table and the extracted data are only in supplements (not read). The text describes some trials' secondary and post hoc findings as 'positive signals' without always stating that the planned primary analysis was null.
analysis.power: Not applicable at review level; the authors judge most included trials underpowered, with small samples and low completion.

interpretation_gap.results_show: 43 small-to-moderate trials of 23 medications, mostly in outpatient men without psychiatric comorbidity, with 38% non-completion and outcomes too heterogeneous to pool. By the review's own Table 4 and text, planned primary analyses were null in all six bupropion trials, both dexamphetamine trials, both topiramate trials, both extended-release naltrexone trials, all four modafinil trials and at least two of four methylphenidate trials; positive results were mostly secondary, post hoc, subgroup, self-reported or completer analyses, plus single positive trials (oral naltrexone in Sweden, riluzole in Iranian men, methylphenidate in an Iranian trial and in one arm of a Finnish three-arm trial, mirtazapine in men who have sex with men).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The conclusion that no medication has convincing results (Abstract; Conclusions) matches the evidence. Gaps: (1) the abstract and Discussion name dexamphetamine, methylphenidate, naltrexone and topiramate as showing the 'most consistent positive findings', but for dexamphetamine and topiramate the primary use outcomes were null in every trial and the signals are secondary or post hoc, as the Discussion itself partly concedes; (2) the Discussion counts the naltrexone implant trial as showing fewer amphetamine-positive urines, whereas Table 4 says there was no difference when amphetamine use was examined alone; (3) the withdrawal section names pexacerfont as a candidate, although Table 4 says that trial did not present amphetamine results separately from opioid results; (4) the Discussion makes clinical statements on choosing inpatient or ambulatory withdrawal settings, while the review found no study comparing settings.

timeline.event: Shoptaw et al., Cochrane review of treatment for amphetamine withdrawal; three of its four trials are among this review's 43 (cited as reference 73).

Bhatt et al., systematic review and meta-analysis of psychostimulants (bupropion, modafinil, methylphenidate, dexamphetamine) for amphetamine and methamphetamine use disorders, searched to August 2016: 17 trials, 14 of which are also among this review's 43 (not cited by this review).
This review: 43 trials to June 2019, no convincing pharmacotherapy. The mirtazapine replication by Coffin et al. (2020) appeared after the search and is described in the Discussion but not included.
ADAPT-2 trial of injectable naltrexone plus oral bupropion, described in this review as completed with results pending

Acheson et al., systematic review and meta-analysis of medications for methamphetamine withdrawal from the same group; shares four trials with this review (Jittiwutikan 1997, Kongsakon 2005, Cruickshank 2008, Lee 2013).

replication.where_it_stands: A comprehensive inventory of the trial literature to mid-2019 and an accurate statement that no medication was established. It is not a quantitative synthesis and its trial-level risk-of-bias judgments are not in the article. It overlaps heavily with other reviews: four trials with Acheson et al. (2023), the mirtazapine trial by Colfax et al. (2011), and 14 of the 17 psychostimulant trials in Bhatt et al. (2016), so these reviews cannot be counted as independent support for the same conclusion. Three trials that Bhatt et al. included (Das 2010, bupropion in men who have sex with men; Konstenius 2010 and 2014, methylphenidate in amphetamine dependence with ADHD) are not among this review's 43, without explanation, and the two reviews summarize the same methylphenidate trial (Ling 2014) differently (Bhatt: lower odds of a methamphetamine-positive urine at week 14; this review: no difference by urine).

funding.funder: National Centre for Clinical Research on Emerging Drugs (NCCRED), funded by the Australian Government Department of Health; NCCRED paid the open-access fee.
funding.declared_conflicts: One author (Lintzeris) has received research funding from Camurus and served on advisory boards for Mundipharma, Camurus and Indivior; the other three declare none.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from NCCRED, St Vincent's Hospital Alcohol and Drug Service, NDARC (UNSW), the University of Sydney, South Eastern Sydney Local Health District and the NSW Drug and Alcohol Clinical Research and Improvement Network. One author (Ezard) is an author of the cited lisdexamfetamine trial protocol (reference 68), so the review's endorsement of agonist approaches comes partly from investigators of an agonist trial then in progress; recorded as a flag for closer reading.

what_would_settle_it: Adequately powered, multi-site placebo-controlled trials of the leading candidates (agonist treatment above all) with a harmonized primary outcome (for example change in use days and proportion of negative urine samples), inclusion of women and people with common psychiatric and substance comorbidity, verified adherence and full adverse-event reporting; and an updated, registered systematic review that pools comparable outcomes with a standard risk-of-bias tool.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population, medication, control and use-related outcomes stated.
Restriction to randomized trials and exclusion of laboratory studies are stated but not explained.

AMSTAR 2 partial yes for item 4 requires at least two databases, the search strategy, and a justification of any publication restriction. The first two are met (PubMed, EMBASE, CINAHL and SCOPUS, the basic strategy printed in the Methods with an example in a supplement, reference lists of selected articles checked, no start-date limit, last search 19 June 2019), but the search was restricted to text in English and neither the Methods nor the Limitations give a reason, so the item fails. No trial registries, no grey literature and no expert contact either; the search ended about nine months before the issue date.
Two reviewers independently, third for disputes.
Two reviewers on identical spreadsheets, compared for consistency.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: No list of excluded full texts in the article; the PRISMA figure is an image and the supplements described do not include one.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 4 gives dose, duration, sample, design and results for every trial; primary outcome and follow-up are not given consistently.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No validated instrument. The Methods name the features assessed as allocation of participants, blinding of participants or personnel, study sample, completion rates, analysis of outcomes, overstated conclusions and funding; allocation concealment, blinding of outcome assessors and selective outcome reporting are not among them, and the Results report only that allocation was by random assignment and that all but three trials were double-blind. AMSTAR 2 requires unconcealed allocation and lack of blinding of participants and assessors even for partial yes, so the item is a no. The per-trial considerations sit in an unread supplement (Supplementary Table 1 and Supplementary Data), which the senior author may wish to check, but the technique itself is the one the Methods describe.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Government or academic 28, pharmaceutical funding or drug supply 10, not stated 4, unfunded 1.
No meta-analysis: the Methods state that the disparity of reported outcomes and measures prohibited pooling and that the review is a qualitative, narrative report.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No pooled estimate exists to test.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: AMSTAR 2 item 13 is yes or no. Judged yes: the Summary of Evidence and the Conclusions both attribute the absence of convincing results to small, biased samples and low completion, and that framing carries the recommendation that no medication can be recommended. The weakness kept in view: the agents named as showing the most consistent signals are not individually weighed against the completer, post hoc and self-report analyses that produced those signals.
Heterogeneity of outcomes, populations, settings and use-frequency cut-offs is discussed at length.

No meta-analysis, so the AMSTAR 2 response is no meta-analysis conducted. Worth recording separately that small-study and publication bias are not discussed anywhere in the review, which matters for a narrative inventory that names promising signals.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported

risk_of_bias.reasoning: AMSTAR 2 critical items are 2, 4, 7, 9, 11, 13 and 15; items 11, 12 and 15 are answered no meta-analysis, because the review states that disparate outcomes prohibited pooling. After the second reading four critical items are answered no: no protocol or registration (2); a search restricted to English without justification and without registries or grey literature (4); no list of excluded full texts (7); and a risk-of-bias assessment whose stated features omit allocation concealment, assessor blinding and selective outcome reporting (9). More than one critical flaw gives critically low confidence under AMSTAR 2, so the rating is unchanged, now resting on four flaws rather than two. Item 13 is yes, items 1, 5, 6, 10, 14 and 16 are yes, item 3 is no and item 8 is partly met. The review remains useful as a transparent, duplicate-screened inventory of 43 trials with their designs and headline results; its narrative ranking of promising agents should not be cited as evidence of efficacy, and claims about specific agents should cite the trials themselves or a quantitative synthesis. Publication bias is not discussed anywhere in the review, which is worth remembering wherever it names signals.

key_findings.finding: 43 randomized trials published 1994 to 2019 met the criteria, randomizing 4065 participants and testing 23 medications or combinations; 40 (93.0%) were double-blind and 39 (90.7%) placebo-controlled by the review's count; 32 (74.4%) were outpatient and 23 (53.5%) were in the USA.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results; Results › Study Selection and Characteristics; Table 2; Table 3
key_findings.note: The text says publication years were 1995 to 2019, but included reference 36 is from 1994.

key_findings.finding: Outcomes were too disparate to pool: 55 distinct primary outcome measures were used 93 times (abstinence 51 times, 41 of them by urine screen analysed in 16 different ways) and 75 secondary measures 158 times.
key_findings.locator: Results › Outcomes and Measures, 1st paragraph; Table 5; Methods, last paragraph

key_findings.finding: In the 38 trials reporting completion, 2298 of 3733 randomized participants (61.6%) completed; women were 29.7% of all participants; 9 trials enrolled men only; 34 trials (79.1%) excluded people with depression or psychosis or taking antidepressants or antipsychotics.
key_findings.locator: Results › Study Selection and Characteristics, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Risk of Bias Within and Across Studies

key_findings.finding: Only 3 of 43 trials (7%) provided information on adverse or serious adverse events, by the review's count; adherence was not reported in 11 trials and ranged from 21% to 100% where reported, with self-report exceeding objective measures (74% versus 42%; 74.7% versus 48.5% by electronic caps).
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Limitations, 2nd paragraph; Results › Outcomes and Measures, last paragraph

key_findings.finding: Trial funding: government or academic 28 (65.1%); pharmaceutical funding or drug supply 10 (23.3%); not stated 4 (9.3%); unfunded 1.
key_findings.locator: Results › Risk of Bias Within and Across Studies, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Bupropion (6 trials): none showed a difference in abstinence or use on the planned primary analysis. The positive signals were all post hoc, subgroup or secondary findings: in one trial a post hoc split by baseline use gave an odds ratio of 2.8 (p < 0.0001) for a methamphetamine-free week among people with light baseline use, with no difference among those with heavier use; in a second trial a planned subgroup with fewer than 18 use days in the past 30 gained abstinent weeks, a further subgroup analysis found more methamphetamine-free weeks in men irrespective of baseline use, and later analysis singled out men with low baseline use (odds ratios 1.39 and 1.34, p <= 0.001) and women without depression and with low baseline use (1.27, p = 0.02); a third trial reported a higher mean number of participants with negative urines on bupropion as a secondary result, with very low medication adherence (Table 4). Bupropion also reduced cigarette smoking in the trial that measured it.
key_findings.locator: Results › Antidepressants, 3rd to 5th paragraphs; Table 4 (bupropion rows)

key_findings.finding: Sertraline (1 trial, 229 participants, with or without contingency management) showed no benefit; the sertraline-only arm was less likely to reach 3-week abstinence and more likely to have methamphetamine-positive urines than the other arms, with more adverse events and early terminations.

Dexamphetamine (2 trials, 49 and 60 participants): no difference in methamphetamine use on planned analyses; reductions in withdrawal, craving or dependence scores were secondary or post hoc, in outpatients who continued to use; longer retention in one trial.
key_findings.locator: Results › Central Nervous System Stimulants, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 4

key_findings.finding: Methylphenidate (3 dedicated trials plus one arm of a three-arm trial): no difference in abstinence in a 79-participant trial with 34% completion; null planned analysis but fewer self-reported use episodes in a secondary analysis of a 110-participant trial; lower craving and fewer positive urines at week 10 in a 56-participant Iranian trial; fewer amphetamine-positive urines than placebo in the Finnish three-arm trial, whose aripiprazole arm did worse than placebo and was stopped early.
key_findings.locator: Results › Central Nervous System Stimulants, 3rd to 6th paragraphs; Atypical Antipsychotics; Table 4

key_findings.finding: Naltrexone (5 trials): no difference by urine in the two extended-release injection trials; reduced self-reported use in a completer analysis of 37 of 52 participants; fewer amphetamine-positive urines with oral naltrexone in a Swedish trial; the implant trial reduced combined opioid and amphetamine use.
key_findings.note: Table 4 says the implant trial found no difference when amphetamine use was examined alone, while the Discussion counts it as sharing the Swedish trial's positive amphetamine result.

key_findings.finding: Modafinil (4 trials) showed no difference in use, adherence or retention; topiramate (2 trials) showed no difference on primary use outcomes, with secondary reductions in use or addiction severity; aripiprazole alone (2 trials) showed no difference in use.
key_findings.locator: Results › Other Central Nervous System Agents; Anticonvulsants; Atypical Antipsychotics; Table 4

key_findings.finding: Mirtazapine (3 trials): reduced methamphetamine-positive urines and sexual risk behaviour in 60 men who have sex with men (Colfax 2011); no difference in retention or withdrawal in a 31-participant withdrawal trial; lower withdrawal scores in a 20-participant unblinded trial in a correctional facility.

Single positive trials: riluzole in 86 Iranian men (higher retention and end-of-treatment abstinence; smokers of more than 3 days a week excluded); pexacerfont reduced craving but not abstinence in 51 men with heroin or methamphetamine dependence, with results not separated by drug.
key_findings.locator: Results › Glutamatergic Agents; CRF1 Antagonist; Table 4
key_findings.note: The riluzole trial is given as n = 74 in the Discussion's withdrawal section.

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that no pharmacotherapy yielded convincing results, while naming stimulant agonists (dexamphetamine, methylphenidate), naltrexone and topiramate as the most consistent positive signals.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results and Conclusions; Discussion › Summary of Evidence; Reduction in Use, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: On amineptine, the review states that it has never been approved by the US Food and Drug Administration and has been suspended in other jurisdictions because of liver toxicity and liability to non-medical use. No date and no reference are given for either statement.
key_findings.note: Relevant to any claim that dates the withdrawal of amineptine: this review, by the same group as acheson_2023, gives no year, so it does not corroborate the 1999 date that review states.

reporting_issues.issue: The list of trials without a placebo control is given as references 36, 49, 61 and 66, but Table 4 describes reference 49 (PROMETA protocol) and reference 61 (sertraline, with placebo arms) as placebo-controlled, and describes reference 24 (buprenorphine versus methadone) as having no control group at all.
reporting_issues.consequence: The count of placebo-controlled trials (39) is unreliable, and one included trial does not meet the review's own requirement of a control group.

reporting_issues.issue: The imipramine trial (reference 36) is included although only 32 of its 183 participants (17%) were methamphetamine-dependent and the rest cocaine-dependent, contradicting the exclusion of studies enrolling primarily non-amphetamine or non-methamphetamine-dependent participants; the same trial dates from 1994, while the text gives the publication range as 1995 to 2019.
reporting_issues.consequence: The eligibility criteria were not applied consistently; the trial's results mostly concern cocaine.

reporting_issues.issue: Analysis descriptions conflict between Table 4 and the text: Table 4 calls the amineptine trial (reference 43) intention-to-treat while the text says its results came from a completer analysis of 29; Table 4 calls the buprenorphine-methadone trial (reference 24) intention-to-treat while the text lists it as not analysed by intention to treat; Table 4 calls the topiramate trial (reference 55) a completer analysis while the text does not list it among non-intention-to-treat trials. Table 4 marks the adolescent bupropion trial (reference 39) as not blinded while the text lists it among double-blind trials.
reporting_issues.consequence: The summary percentages for intention-to-treat analysis (83%) and double-blinding (93%) cannot be relied on exactly.

reporting_issues.issue: The naltrexone implant trial (reference 63) is reported in Table 4 as showing no difference in amphetamine use when examined alone, but the Discussion cites it as sharing the oral-naltrexone trial's finding of fewer amphetamine-positive urines.
reporting_issues.consequence: The naltrexone 'signal' is weaker than the Discussion states; claims should rely on the Swedish oral trial alone, and on later trials.

reporting_issues.issue: The same trials are described differently in different places: the modafinil withdrawal trial has 20 participants in Table 4 and 19 in the text; the riluzole trial has 86 participants in Table 4 and the Results and 74 in the withdrawal section, and 50 mg twice daily in Table 4 but once daily in the text; mirtazapine in the 2005 trial is 15 to 30 mg in Table 4 and 15 to 60 mg in the text; ondansetron is twice daily in Table 4 and once daily in the text.
reporting_issues.consequence: Study conditions should be taken from the primary trials, not from this review.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says the first mirtazapine trial in men who have sex with men had adherence below 50% by both electronic caps and self-report, but the adherence paragraph gives that trial's self-reported adherence as 74.7% (48.5% by caps).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; adherence was low by the objective measure only.

reporting_issues.issue: Nine trials are said to have enrolled only men, 'not all of these by design', and later the same nine are said to have excluded women by design.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor inconsistency in describing the under-representation of women.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion describes the primary outcome of the then-pending naltrexone-bupropion trial (NCT03078075) as the percentage of methamphetamine-negative urines over 12 weeks; the encyclopedia's card for the published trial (sc_trivedi_2021) records the primary outcome as a urine-defined response in the last 2 weeks of each 6-week stage.
reporting_issues.consequence: The review's description of that trial should not be used; the trial report and its registry are the sources.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 5 lists 'participant satisfaction' as a primary outcome domain measured by the type and number of adverse events.
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably a table alignment error; no effect on the conclusions.

reporting_issues.issue: The bupropion signal is attributed to different trials in different sections. The Discussion (Reduction in Use, 5th paragraph) says that bupropion reduced use in people with light baseline use or in men and cites reference 60 (Shoptaw et al., 2008) alone, whereas the Results (Antidepressants, 4th paragraph) attribute the male-subgroup finding and the odds ratios of 1.39, 1.34 and 1.27 to reference 33 (Elkashef et al., 2008).
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader following the Discussion would cite the wrong trial. Claims about a bupropion signal in men should cite Elkashef et al. (2008) directly, and the subgroup character of the finding should travel with the citation.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC7125061 (all sections, Tables 1 to 5 rendered as text, author contributions, funding and conflict statements, and reference list read; Figure 1 (PRISMA flow) is an image and its values were not extracted; supplementary material 1 to 3 (search example, extended study table, extracted data) not read).

disagreements.first_pass: signals were confined to post hoc or subgroup analyses in people with light baseline use (odds ratio 2.8 … in one trial; odds ratios 1.27 to 1.39 in subgroups of another) and to reduced cigarette smoking
disagreements.reviewer: signals were not confined to people with light baseline use: the Results also report a male-subgroup signal irrespective of baseline use (Elkashef 2008) and Table 4 records a secondary finding in Heinzerling 2014
disagreements.resolution: Rewritten. Checked at Results › Antidepressants ¶4: the male-only subgroup is reported as a separate additional subgroup analysis, not as part of the light-use split, and the odds ratios of 1.39 and 1.34 are for men with low baseline use, with 1.27 for women without depression and with low use. Table 4 confirms the Heinzerling 2014 secondary result (more participants with negative urines, very low adherence). The finding now names all three trials and labels each signal post hoc, subgroup or secondary; the locator is extended to the bupropion rows of Table 4.

disagreements.reviewer: should be 'no', not 'partial yes': AMSTAR 2's partial yes needs the publication restriction justified, and the English-only restriction is not justified
disagreements.resolution: Changed to no. Checked in the source: the Methods state that the search was limited to text in the English language and give no reason, and the Limitations section (comorbidity exclusions, outcome disparity, adherence, definitions of efficacy, use cut-offs, population restrictions, the amphetamine-methamphetamine pooling) never returns to it. AMSTAR 2 requires the restriction to be justified even for partial yes. Item 4 is critical, so this adds a critical flaw.

disagreements.reviewer: should be 'no' on the article's evidence (concealment and assessor blinding are not assessed); alternatively 'no-information', since the trial-level judgments are only in the unseen supplement
disagreements.resolution: Changed to no, which is the reader's primary reading. AMSTAR 2 item 9 concerns the technique, and the Methods state it in full: the list omits allocation concealment, assessor blinding and selective outcome reporting, and partial yes already requires the first two. The editors' 'no-information' extension is for an item only an unread supplement could decide, which is not the case when the article itself states the method, so it was not used; the note records that the per-trial table is in a supplement. Item 9 is critical, so this adds a critical flaw.

disagreements.reviewer: 'partial yes' is not an AMSTAR 2 response for item 13; would record 'yes', keeping the card's point about the named signals in the note
disagreements.resolution: Changed to yes. AMSTAR 2 offers partial yes only for items 2, 4, 7, 8 and 9 (METHODS §5.3). Decided from the source: Discussion › Summary of Evidence states that the trials were generally small, the samples biased and completion low, which is why no pharmacotherapy can be recommended, and the Conclusions repeat it. The reservation about the ranking of signals stays in the note and in the interpretation gap.

disagreements.first_pass: the three items were left out of the domain list, their inapplicability explained in the reasoning only
disagreements.reviewer: items 11, 12 and 15 should be recorded as 'no meta-analysis' rather than omitted, so that the domain list is complete
disagreements.resolution: Added with judgment 'no-meta-analysis', the response AMSTAR 2 provides for exactly these three items (METHODS §5.3). Confirmed in the source: the last paragraph of the Methods states that the disparity of outcomes and measures prohibited meta-analysis and that the report is qualitative. The observation that publication bias is nowhere discussed is kept in the note on item 15.

disagreements.first_pass: critically-low (two critical items failing, two more partly met)
disagreements.reviewer: agrees with critically low confidence; proposes item-level changes that do not alter it
disagreements.resolution: Overall recomputed under the AMSTAR 2 critical-item rule after items 4, 9 and 13 were decided from the source and items 11, 12 and 15 recorded as no meta-analysis: critical items 2, 4, 7 and 9 are no, 13 is yes, 11 and 15 are no meta-analysis. More than one critical flaw gives critically low confidence, so critically-low stands.

disagreements.reviewer: missed: the Discussion attributes the signal in people with light baseline use or in men to Shoptaw 2008 alone, whereas the Results attribute the male-subgroup finding to Elkashef 2008
disagreements.resolution: Added as a reporting issue after checking both places: Discussion › Reduction in Use ¶5 cites reference 60 only, while Results › Antidepressants ¶4 attributes the male subgroup and the three odds ratios to reference 33. The reference list confirms 33 = Elkashef et al. 2008 and 60 = Shoptaw et al. 2008.

disagreements.reviewer: missed: the review says amineptine was never FDA-approved and 'has been suspended in other jurisdictions', with no date and no reference; relevant to cl_meth_withdrawal_medication
disagreements.resolution: Added as a key finding. Confirmed at Results › Antidepressants, 1st paragraph: the sentence carries no reference marker and no year, so the card can record that the second review from this group says nothing that corroborates the 1999 withdrawal date.
